title: Verification Receipt
description: A machine-checkable record of a single verification decision (a workload approval, a compute registration, an audit certificate, a license grant, or a license revocation), designed so that a legal or treaty dispute-resolution process can reference a receipt_id and get a self-contained, independently checkable artifact -- not just a line in someone's private log. This is the 'bind verification to governance' half of the trust-composition problem: the trust_composition/ tool checks whether an architecture's independence claim holds; this schema is what the architecture's OUTPUT has to look like for that claim to be worth anything to a court, a treaty body, or an auditor who wasn't in the room.

schema_version.description: Schema version this receipt was produced against, e.g. '1.0'. A verifier must refuse to interpret a receipt against a schema_version it doesn't recognize rather than guessing at forward compatibility.

receipt_id.description: Globally unique identifier for this receipt, stable forever. This is the string a treaty or dispute-resolution reference points to.

receipt_type.description: What kind of decision this receipt records.

issued_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of issuance, per whatever clock the issuing system uses (production systems: real time; this repo's demo system: a simulated clock, disclosed in producer_note).

subject_id.description: The unit, organization, or workload this receipt is about.

statement.description: The actual assertion, in plain language a non-specialist reader (a judge, a treaty officer) can act on -- not just a machine code.

confidence.description: How confident the issuing process is in the statement. 1.0 only for claims that are exact by construction (e.g. a cryptographic verification), not for statistical or judgment-based claims.

basis.description: One sentence on WHY: which mechanism produced this claim (e.g. 'k-of-n signature quorum', 'Wilson-score statistical bound over an audited sample', 'LLM-based policy review'). A reader deciding how much to trust the claim needs to know this.

hash.description: SHA-256 hex digest of this receipt's own canonicalized content, chained to prev_hash.

prev_hash.description: Hash of the immediately preceding receipt in this issuer's chain. All-zero for the first receipt in a chain.

scheme.description: 'single-signer' MUST only be used for systems that have not implemented multi-party issuance; per the trust-composition analysis in this repo, single-signer schemes have a min_attack of 1 against any claimed threshold above 1 and should be treated as unattested for governance purposes.

signer_role.description: e.g. 'Operating Lab', 'Independent Auditor' -- the ROLE, since governance bodies care about who is structurally represented, not just headcount.

signature.description: Base64-encoded signature over the canonicalized claim + subject + issued_at.

public_key_fingerprint.description: Truncated hash of the signer's public key, for out-of-band identity confirmation.

allOf.description: Structural note (not machine-enforced by this schema alone; see validator.py for the cross-field check): len(signatures) must be >= required_quorum, and signer_ids among signatures must be distinct, for a receipt to be considered CONSUMMATED rather than merely proposed.

instrument_ref.description: Which treaty, agreement, or policy this receipt is issued under. A receipt with no instrument_ref is evidence of nothing in particular to anyone outside the issuing organization.

retention_until.description: This receipt MUST remain retrievable and verifiable until this date, per the governing instrument's retention rule.

dispute_process.description: How to contest this receipt's claim -- a process name, contact, or reference, not necessarily a URL.

supersedes.description: receipt_id of a prior receipt this one revises or renews, if any -- the semantic-level analog of evidence_chain.prev_hash.

producer_note.description: Optional free text for anything a reader needs to correctly weigh this receipt that the structured fields don't capture -- e.g. 'issued against a simulated clock in a demonstration system, not a production deployment.'
